title: Chicago trio length, guitar versus banjo, his brother
summary: The Chicago trio was his longest group; he played electric guitar and returned to banjo only in the mid-1950s. His oldest brother played banjo in Robert Clark's band.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: you know, yeah. So you were working with that trio for quite a while, I guess.
Well, yeah, that's the longest group I've worked with the whole I was in Chicago.
How long was that? Do you work with them?
Well, we started up, I'd say around about, oh, around about 40, and we stayed together, I think, about 44, 45, maybe part of 46.
Gee, still with the same three guys?
Yeah, we created quite a reputation around Chicago, at least playing like cocktail lounge and cabaret.
What did you play then, banjo or guitar?
No, I was playing electric guitar.
Yeah, when I went to Chicago, I had put the banjo down there.
So, you didn't get a chance to play the banjo until you got back to New Orleans.

Oh, I'd say I'd just start playing the banjo, let's see, I was at the paddock, that was, what did I say, 45, 55, 56, 57, and that was probably when I went back on the banjo, I mean, and there was just a few numbers I played then because the people were more crazy about, electric guitar and then we were working with a trio, you know. Every once in a while I used to sit in with the band, with Bill Matthews band sometimes, you know, just sitting a few minutes to play with them.
Hey, going back to you really early, did you, anybody else in the family ever play an intro besides your daddy?

Yeah, my oldest brother, like the one I said, I was teaching him bands, he played for a while, he played with a band around the 30s there called the Robert Clark Band. That was a 10-piece band they had in those days. And they played for around the New Orleans Wild and had a lot of, a few out of town dates and everything.
